nameStory: The Black-dotted Glyph gets its name from the distinctive dark spots that pepper its forewings like tiny ink dots on parchment. The word 'glyph' refers to carved or inscribed symbols, perfectly describing how these moths look like they're decorated with mysterious ancient markings.
description: The Black-dotted Glyph is a medium-sized moth in the cutworm family, one of New England's many nocturnal fliers. Like other owlet moths, it has a sturdy, triangular silhouette when at rest with wings folded tent-like over its body. Its most striking feature is the pattern of dark spots scattered across pale forewings, giving it an almost hieroglyphic appearance. Adults typically measure about an inch across when their wings are spread.

idTips.label: Black dots on forewings
idTips.description: Multiple small, round black spots scattered across pale gray or whitish forewings, like someone dabbed ink with a fine brush

idTips.label: Triangular resting posture
idTips.description: When at rest, forms a distinctive tent shape with wings folded over the body, creating a sharp triangular outline

idTips.label: Pale coloration
idTips.description: Overall light gray to off-white appearance that feels soft and powdery to the touch if handled gently

idTips.label: Medium size
idTips.description: About the size of your thumbnail when wings are folded, with a compact, sturdy body typical of cutworm moths

idTips.label: Nocturnal activity
idTips.description: Active after dark, often found resting on tree bark or building walls during the day where they blend in surprisingly well

habitat: Black-dotted Glyphs prefer wooded areas throughout New England, from mixed deciduous-coniferous forests to woodland edges and clearings. They're commonly found in areas with oak, maple, and birch trees, where their caterpillars likely feed on various shrubs and herbaceous plants. Look for adults resting on tree bark, building walls, or drawn to porch lights in suburban areas near wooded habitats.

seasonality.spring: Adults may begin emerging in late spring, but they're not commonly observed until early summer. Any spring sightings are usually late in the season.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight time for adults, when they're most active and visible. Look for them at porch lights or resting on pale surfaces during the day.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity continues into early fall, though numbers typically decline. Late-season individuals may appear more worn with faded markings.
seasonality.winter: Adults are not present; the species overwinters as eggs or early larval stages, hidden away until the following growing season.

funFact: Despite being called 'cutworm moths,' many species in this family, including the Black-dotted Glyph, don't actually have caterpillars that cut plants at ground level - that behavior is mainly limited to a few notorious agricultural pest species, while most family members are harmless woodland creatures.
confusionNotes: Many small pale moths can look similar at first glance, but the Black-dotted Glyph's scattered dot pattern is quite distinctive. Remember: if you see clear black dots like someone flicked ink from a pen, you've likely found your glyph.
contextualKnowledge: This moth is also sometimes called the 'black-dotted lithacodia' in older field guides, referring to a former genus name. The family name 'Noctuidae' literally means 'night owls,' reflecting their nocturnal habits.
compareHints: As the only Maliattha species in New England, the Black-dotted Glyph stands alone in its genus here. Among other small pale noctuids, it's distinguished by its particularly clear and numerous black spots - many similar species have more subtle markings, wavy lines, or solid patches rather than the distinct dotted pattern that makes this species so recognizable.
